Part 4 of 4

Full Circle

By the Twice Baked AI Team

Post 3 ended with a real success: a physically grounded noise model, working directly on raw sensor data, that closed the fidelity gap every earlier method in this series had struggled with. That success didn’t end this project’s search for a better approach. It changed what the remaining, harder problem actually was.

This closing post covers two more method families, self-supervised training and classical domain adaptation, and then something more interesting than either alone: a finding that showed up independently across three completely different approaches, converging on the exact same wall.

The new problem, once the noise model was solid

Every method in this series has operated on a spectrum between two failure modes named back in Post 1: erasing real detail, and inventing detail that isn’t there. Once the physics-based noise model from Post 3 made the data trustworthy, a sharper, more specific version of that same tension came into focus: how aggressively should a restoration model be allowed to change an image it isn’t fully certain about?

Push a model to denoise harder, and you risk it also touching regions that were already fine, a direct violation of the “clean in, clean out” requirement established back in Post 1. Hold a model back to protect already-clean regions, and you risk leaving real noise uncorrected where it’s needed most. This project calls this the R1 tension, after the specific requirement it threatens. What makes it worth an entire closing post is what happened when three unrelated methods were each pushed to find out where their own limit was.

Self-supervised learning: training without any clean reference at all

Every method described so far, in this post and the three before it, assumed access to a real clean reference image at training time, even the physics-based approach in Post 3 needs a real clean raw acquisition to synthetically degrade. Self-supervised methods remove that requirement entirely: they train a denoising network using only noisy real acquisitions, with no clean reference in the loop at all.

This project used an approach called Recorrupted-to-Recorrupted, or R2R, a real, published technique.1

For contrast: the classical VST+BM3D control arm this section’s result is compared against, a well-established signal-processing technique requiring no training at all.

The core trick is elegant: take a real noisy image, and deliberately add a known amount of additional noise to it, twice, in two different, statistically independent ways. Train a network to map one of these “recorrupted” versions to the other. It’s mathematically equivalent, in expectation, to training on real noisy/clean pairs, without ever needing a clean image to exist.

The R2R mechanism. No clean image appears anywhere in this diagram, and that’s the entire point.

An illustrative walk through the same mechanism, using the real reference image used throughout this series as a stand-in for a noisy real acquisition. Only the noisy image and its two recorrupted versions are ever used, no clean reference appears in the actual training process.

This project’s specific implementation of R2R works on raw sensor data, the same domain established in Post 3, using the same noise physics to construct the two recorrupted versions correctly. That detail matters: R2R’s mathematical guarantee depends on the added noise being correctly characterized, which is only possible because Post 3’s physics-based noise law already existed to characterize it correctly.

A real, three-way comparison

Rather than testing R2R in isolation, the team ran it directly alongside two other approaches on the same real data: the classical VST+BM3D control arm introduced back in Post 2, and a standard baseline trained the conventional way on synthetic pairs.

A real comparison at a representative dose level: clean reference, noisy input, baseline, R2R, and classical VST+BM3D, all on the same real data.

The same five-way comparison run at full dose, where the correct answer is “change nothing at all”, is the actual R1 test in practice:

The R1 test, made concrete: at full dose, the image is already clean. Any method that visibly changes it here is failing the requirement, regardless of how good it looks at lower doses.

Real, tracked metrics over training confirmed the self-supervised approach was learning something genuine, not just memorizing noise:

Real tracked progress on two calibration phantoms. The restored result (blue and orange lines) climbs clearly above the untouched baseline (gray) on both, confirming genuine learning, not a fluke.

The same method’s real output at full image scale, confirming the result holds beyond the small regions typically used for close inspection.

Where it actually stopped

Pushed far enough, this self-supervised approach reached a real, measured milestone: it became the first learned method in this project’s history to outscore the plain classical control arm on a specific denoising-strength measure. That’s a genuine result. It also, at that same operating point, showed the over-smoothing measure (the R1-violation signal from Post 1) climbing past 78%, high enough that the team stopped the run deliberately rather than continue toward an already-scheduled longer training extension. Not a failure in the sense of broken code or a bad implementation, a real, working method that hit the same wall from a completely different direction than the other two.

Classical domain adaptation: making a public dataset usable

The second thread in this post has nothing to do with noise directly. It’s about a different, earlier limitation: getting more anatomical variety into the training data by using a large public chest X-ray dataset (VinDr, freely available for research use) alongside this project’s own smaller in-house collection.

The problem is that images from a different source look different, different tone curves, different contrast handling, different average brightness, even before any degradation is considered.

The actual risk this section addresses: without harmonization, a model can learn to correct a style mismatch instead of the dose difference it’s actually meant to fix.

Training on a mismatched blend risks teaching a model to fix a difference that has nothing to do with dose. Five classical harmonization techniques, going back decades in the broader image-processing literature, were tested directly against each other on real data:

Five real harmonization techniques, tested on the same real image. Reinhard color transfer, Nyúl-Udupa landmark matching, Pitié N-PDF distribution transport, Laplacian pyramid matching, and a polynomial tone-curve method, each a real, established technique from the wider image-processing literature.2

An illustrative animation of the Laplacian pyramid method’s core idea: match tone at multiple scales, not all at once.

The Laplacian pyramid method, which matches tone separately at multiple frequency scales rather than with one global adjustment, was the team’s own recommendation from this real comparison, consistent with a theme that’s run through this whole series: treating different frequency content differently tends to outperform one-size-fits-all corrections.

The convergence

Here is the finding this whole closing post has been building toward. Three methods, developed and tested independently, using entirely different mechanisms, arrived at versions of the exact same wall:

Self-supervised learning, classical signal processing, and standard supervised training. Three different mechanisms, one shared limit.

An illustrative visualization of the convergence, built up one method at a time. The shared upward shape is the point, not the exact curve values.

This convergence is a genuinely stronger finding than any one method’s result on its own. If only one approach hit this ceiling, you could reasonably suspect something specific to that architecture or training recipe. When three unrelated approaches, one with no clean reference at all, one with no learning at all, and one with the standard synthetic-pair recipe from Post 3, all hit close to the same wall, the far more likely explanation is that the wall is a property of the underlying problem itself, not a fixable flaw in any one method.

What this history adds up to

Every method family across all four posts, and where it actually ended up. No single row is the whole story.

Four posts, roughly a dozen distinct methods, spanning hand-written rules, three separate generative-modeling philosophies, a from-scratch physics model, self-supervised learning, and classical signal processing. No single method is the tidy hero of this story. The physics-based approach from Post 3 remains the current, most reliable foundation this project builds on, and even it doesn’t fully resolve the tension this closing post describes.

That’s a genuinely different kind of ending than “and then we solved it.” We think it’s a more honest one. The recurring lesson across every post in this series, hand-written noise models that needed real calibration, generative methods that each failed in a specific, diagnosable way, physics that needed careful, patient recovery from a rendering pipeline that obscures it, and now three independent methods agreeing on where the real difficulty lives, is that progress here has come from characterizing the problem precisely, one honest measurement at a time, more consistently than it’s come from any single clever architecture.

Before closing, one last piece of honesty: this account was checked, twice, against our own project’s surviving records before we published it, and where different internal sources disagreed with each other on a detail, we’ve tried to say so plainly in this series rather than picking whichever version made for a cleaner story.

If a future chapter in this history gets written, it’ll pick up exactly here: at a wall three independent methods found the same way, with no single fix yet in hand.

This concludes the current chapters of an ongoing series documenting the dataset-creation history behind our low-dose X-ray restoration research.

  1. Recorrupted-to-Recorrupted: Unsupervised Deep Learning for Image Denoising, Pang, Zheng, Quan & Ji, CVPR 2021. openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2021/papers/Pang_Recorrupted-to-Recorrupted_Unsupervised_Deep_Learning_for_Image_Denoising_CVPR_2021_paper.pdf↩︎
